title: SolanaGuard AI: Understand Before You Sign
author: Samuel Emmanuel
summary: What if you could understand what a Solana transaction is doing before deciding whether to approve it? That question inspired me to build SolanaGuard AI , an AI-powered Solana transaction security assistant. I built this project as an individual developer while participating in a Solana hackathon. My goal was to explore how blockchain data and AI could work together to make transaction information easier to understand, especially for people who may not be comfortable reading raw blockchain transaction details. 🔗 Explore SolanaGuard AI 🚀 Live Demo: Try SolanaGuard AI 💻 GitHub Repository: View the source code Understand Before You Sign. The problem Interacting with blockchain applications often involves approving transactions without fully understanding what is happening behind the scenes. A transaction may contain multiple instructions, interact with different programs, or involve changes to token permissions and account authorities. For experienced developers, inspecting these details may be manageable. For beginners and everyday users, however, understanding what they mean can be difficult. I wanted to explore a solution that could help users inspect transaction details and understand potential warning signs before making a decision. What I built SolanaGuard AI allows users to submit a Solana transaction signature for analysis. The application retrieves transaction information from the Solana Devnet, examines available transaction details, applies deterministic risk checks, and uses AI to explain the findings in plain language. The main idea is simple: Understand Before You Sign. Some of the features include: Solana Devnet transaction retrieval. Transaction status and instruction analysis. Examination of available account and token-related information. Rule-based risk scoring. Evidence-based security findings. AI-powered explanations to make technical findings easier to understand. One important design decision was separating the risk engine from the AI explanation layer. The risk score is calculated using deterministic rules. AI helps explain the findings; it does not determine or secretly modify the risk score. This distinction matters because an AI-generated explanation should not be treated as verified blockchain evidence. Technology stack Here are the technologies I used: Component Technology Frontend React, Vite, TypeScript Styling Tailwind CSS Backend Python, FastAPI Blockchain data Solana Devnet JSON-RPC AI integration Backboard API HTTP requests Python HTTPX Frontend deployment Vercel Backend deployment Render I chose Python and FastAPI for the backend because I wanted a straightforward way to retrieve and process transaction data while keeping the application modular. Some technical challenges I encountered Building this project was not just about writing code. I also had to understand how the different components communicate. 1. Working with Solana transaction data Retrieving a transaction is only the beginning. Understanding its instructions, accounts, metadata, and token-related information requires careful parsing. I also had to account for missing metadata, unsupported transaction versions, failed transactions, and RPC errors. 2. Designing the risk engine I wanted the application to provide useful warnings without automatically treating unfamiliar programs as malicious. This meant designing transparent rules and attaching evidence to findings rather than making unsupported security claims. 3. Separating AI explanations from verified facts AI can make technical information easier to understand, but it can also produce inaccurate explanations. I designed the system so that deterministic analysis provides the findings and AI helps communicate them. Unknown information should remain unknown rather than being presented as fact. 4. Deployment and CORS Getting the application running locally was one milestone. Deploying the backend to Render and preparing the frontend for Vercel introduced another set of challenges. I encountered a CORS issue while connecting the frontend and backend. Debugging it helped me understand how browser origins, API URLs, and environment variables work together. These challenges reminded me that building a working application involves much more than getting the code to compile. What I learned This project has helped me understand several important concepts: How to interact with Solana through JSON-RPC. How transaction instructions and metadata can be inspected. How to design a rule-based risk analysis system. How to integrate an AI API into a backend application. How to structure a React and FastAPI application. How to debug CORS and environment variable issues. How to deploy a full-stack application using Render and Vercel. I also learned that AI should support security analysis, not replace evidence or create a false sense of security. What SolanaGuard AI does NOT do I think it is important to be transparent about the limitations. SolanaGuard AI does not: Sign or execute transactions. Approve or block wallet transactions. Guarantee that a transaction is safe. Detect every possible scam or malicious program. Replace a professional security audit. It is an analysis assistant intended to help users understand available transaction information and identify potential warning signs. What's next? There is still room to improve the project. Some areas I would like to explore include: Better decoding of supported Solana instructions. More comprehensive token authority and delegation analysis. Additional transaction security heuristics. Improved handling of unknown or unavailable transaction data. More testing with real-world transaction examples. Further improvements to the user experience. Final thoughts Building SolanaGuard AI has been a valuable learning experience. As someone exploring the intersection of AI and blockchain development, this project gave me an opportunity to move beyond tutorials and work on a practical problem. It also reminded me that good AI engineering is not simply about adding an AI API to an application. It is about deciding where AI is useful, where deterministic logic is more appropriate, and how to communicate uncertainty honestly. I'm looking forward to improving the project and learning from feedback from the Solana and developer communities. Understand Before You Sign. If you're building in the Solana ecosystem or exploring AI-powered security tools, I'd love to hear your thoughts.

title: Comment Claude sait-il qu'une citation d'une base de connaissances osFoundry est toujours à jour ?
author: BBT
summary: Voici les outils de base de connaissances qu'un chat Claude ou Claude Code reçoit du serveur MCP d' osFoundry . Ils ont été récupérés avec un tools/list non authentifié le 2026-11-08 et réduits à ce qui compte ici : { "name" : "search_knowledge_base" , "description" : "Search current published articles in one granted knowledge base. Results cite the article ID and updated time; this is a live database read." , "inputSchema" : { "required" : [ "knowledge_base_id" , "query" ], "properties" : { "query" : { "type" : "string" , "minLength" : 2 , "maxLength" : 200 }, "limit" : { "type" : "integer" , "minimum" : 1 , "maximum" : 20 }}}, "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : true }} { "name" : "read_knowledge_article" , "description" : "Read one current published article by ID from a granted knowledge base and return a stable citation." , "inputSchema" : { "required" : [ "knowledge_base_id" , "article_id" ]}, "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : true }} { "name" : "edit_knowledge_article" , "description" : "Replace article content and optionally its title. Supply the version from read_knowledge_article; concurrent changes are rejected." , "inputSchema" : { "required" : [ "knowledge_base_id" , "article_id" , "content" , "expected_version" , "idempotency_key" ]}, "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : false , "destructiveHint" : true , "openWorldHint" : true }} { "name" : "poll_resource_events" , "description" : "Resume from an event sequence for one granted channel, Note, knowledge base, record, or session." , "inputSchema" : { "required" : [ "resource_type" , "resource_id" ], "properties" : { "after_sequence" : { "type" : "integer" , "minimum" : 0 }, "limit" : { "type" : "integer" , "minimum" : 1 , "maximum" : 100 }}}, "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : true }} Quand on lit les descriptions ensemble, le design apparaît de lui-même. Un résultat de recherche porte un ID d'article et une date de mise à jour. Une lecture renvoie "a stable citation" (une citation stable). Une modification exige "the version from read_knowledge_article" (la version issue de read_knowledge_article). Et il existe un journal d'événements par base de connaissances qu'on peut reprendre à partir d'un numéro de séquence. La date de mise à jour de la citation et la version qu'une modification doit indiquer sont, en pratique, le même type de valeur : le propre client d'osFoundry pour ces outils, connected-cloud-tools.ts dans l'application desktop, type expected_version de edit_knowledge_article en format: date-time . Une citation n'est donc pas qu'un pointeur pour le lecteur. C'est un tampon de version que l'agent peut vérifier plus tard et, juste après la lecture, renvoyer comme jeton de compare-and-swap. La suite montre ce que ça apporte, mesuré sur une reconstruction. Que doit contenir une citation ? Trois candidats : Citation Résiste à un changement de titre Montre que le contenu a changé Utilisable comme version d'édition Titre de l'article non non non ID de l'article oui non non ID de l'article + date de mise à jour oui oui oui, si elle est récente Le titre est ce qu'un lecteur humain veut voir, d'où la tentation de citer par le titre seul et de le rechercher plus tard. Mais ça ne détecte qu'un article renommé ou supprimé. Un article dont le texte a changé sous le même titre a l'air correct. L'ID règle le problème des renommages. C'est la date qui permet de vérifier si une citation est périmée. La reconstruction Aucun binaire Claude ne tourne ici. kb_store.py implémente les quatre outils sur sqlite avec les vrais noms, arguments obligatoires et limites (query de 2–200 caractères, limit jusqu'à 20 pour la recherche et jusqu'à 100 pour les événements). Seuls les articles publiés peuvent être recherchés ou lus. Les formes JSON sont propres à la reconstruction, car le vrai serveur ne les renvoie qu'à un client authentifié. La citation est {knowledge_base_id, article_id, updated_at} . Chaque enregistrement écrit un événement {sequence, type, article_id, updated_at} , et edit_knowledge_article est un compare-and-swap sur updated_at avec une table d'idempotence, dans une seule transaction BEGIN IMMEDIATE . sim.py simule une journée de support : 400 articles, 120 questions et 300 enregistrements faits par des personnes sur 8 heures. La popularité suit une courbe de Zipf (s = 0.9). Les 10 premiers articles reçoivent 36.7% des questions et 36.7% des enregistrements, parce que les articles sur lesquels les gens posent des questions sont ceux que les gens n'arrêtent pas de corriger. Parmi les enregistrements, 85% modifient le contenu, 10% changent aussi le titre et 5% dépublient. Pour chaque question, un "Claude" scripté appelle search_knowledge_base , lit les deux premiers résultats avec read_knowledge_article et garde les deux citations. Toutes les heures, il vérifie de trois façons toutes les citations données jusque-là. Seeds 1–5, Python 3.9.6 sur un Apple M1, stdlib uniquement. L'exécution complète prend 25.7 s. À quelle vitesse les citations deviennent-elles périmées ? Cinq seeds, 120 réponses chacune, deux citations par réponse : Heure Citations jusqu'ici Périmées Réponses avec une citation périmée Détectées par le titre seul 1 152 24 (15.8%) 56.6% 5 sur 24 2 298 61 (20.5%) 61.7% 17 sur 61 4 580 165 (28.4%) 72.1% 56 sur 165 6 914 250 (27.4%) 69.4% 84 sur 250 8 1,200 369 (30.8%) 80.2% 152 sur 369 En fin de journée, près d'un tiers des citations pointent vers un article qui a changé depuis que Claude l'a lu, et quatre réponses sur cinq contiennent au moins une citation de ce genre. "Modifié" ne veut pas dire "faux" : une modification peut toucher un paragraphe que la réponse n'a jamais utilisé. Mais personne ne peut savoir lequel sans regarder, et c'est la date dans la citation qui indique à Claude où regarder. La popularité explique l'essentiel. Le run de contrôle répartit les mêmes 300 enregistrements uniformément sur les 400 articles : 13.9% des citations deviennent périmées (167 sur 1,200) et 46.7% des réponses (280 sur 600). Plus ta base de connaissances est utilisée, plus les articles que Claude cite sont ceux qu'on est en train de modifier. La vérification par titre seul a trouvé 152 des 369 citations périmées, soit 41.2%. Il s'agissait uniquement de changements de titre ou de dépublications. Elle ne voit jamais une modification de contenu. Relire chaque article cité, ou interroger le journal ? Coût des vérifications horaires sur la journée, cumulé sur les cinq seeds (40 vérifications) : Stratégie Appels Données renvoyées Par vérification Relancer une recherche sur chaque titre cité 2,426 3,342 KiB 60.6 appels, 83.5 KiB Relire chaque article cité 2,264 3,445 KiB 56.6 appels, 86.1 KiB poll_resource_events depuis un curseur 40 153 KiB 1.0 appel, 3.8 KiB Les deux stratégies basées sur l'ID ont trouvé exactement les mêmes 369 citations périmées que la vérité terrain. Le script le vérifie par un assert à chaque contrôle. La différence, c'est le coût. Relire croît avec le nombre d'articles cités et paie leur texte complet à chaque fois. Le polling croît avec le nombre de changements. Moins de 100 changements par heure tiennent dans une page, donc chaque vérification a été un seul appel, et Claude ne relit que les articles qui ont bougé. Le curseur est un simple entier à conserver entre les tours. Avant le premier poll, l'agent a besoin d'une séquence de départ, soit 0, soit la dernière séquence qu'il a enregistrée avec ses citations. Que se passe-t-il quand Claude modifie avec la version d'une citation ? La deuxième expérience reprend la même journée. Après chaque réponse, Claude modifie le premier article qu'il a cité en passant le updated_at de la citation comme expected_version , après un délai. Cinq seeds, 150 modifications par délai : Délai après la lecture Rejetées, version changée Rejetées, dépublié Nouvel essai après une relecture 20 s 0 (0.0%) 0 — 15 min 30 (20.0%) 2 30 sur 30 enregistrées 1 h 57 (38.0%) 3 57 sur 57 enregistrées 4 h 85 (56.7%) 14 85 sur 85 enregistrées Une citation fait une bonne version d'édition pendant quelques secondes et une mauvaise au bout d'une heure. Les rejets, c'est le système qui fonctionne : chacune de ces écritures aurait sinon remplacé le texte plus récent d'une personne par un contenu construit à partir d'une lecture plus ancienne. La correction est mécanique. Relire, réappliquer le changement sur ce qui est là, écrire avec la nouvelle version. Chaque nouvel essai a réussi. La clé d'idempotence a aussi été testée. Après chaque modification réussie, le même appel avec la même clé a été renvoyé. 409 sur 409 ont renvoyé le premier résultat marqué comme replay et n'ont écrit aucun nouvel événement. Pourquoi osFoundry répond-il uniquement à partir d'articles publiés ? Parce qu'une citation devrait pointer vers quelque chose qu'une personne a décidé être une réponse. Dans l'application desktop, l'onglet Publishing d'un article indique "Published articles are used by this workspace's AI assistant and search. They are not visible outside the workspace." (les articles publiés sont utilisés par l'assistant IA et la recherche de ce workspace, et ne sont pas visibles en dehors). Les brouillons sont invisibles pour search_knowledge_base et read_knowledge_article , et un article dépublié disparaît des deux au prochain appel. Dans la reconstruction, la dépublication écrit un événement comme n'importe quel enregistrement. 19 des 600 modifications différées ci-dessus sont tombées sur un article dépublié, et la vérification signale une telle citation comme disparue, pas comme modifiée. Pourquoi l'outil de modification est-il marqué open-world ? edit_knowledge_article est le seul outil de base de connaissances avec openWorldHint: true . Son effet ne reste pas dans la conversation. L'article enregistré est ce à partir de quoi tous les autres assistants et recherches du workspace répondront ensuite. Les annotations indiquent au client que cet appel modifie un état partagé, et Claude Code demande confirmation avant de l'exécuter, sauf si tu l'as autorisé. osFoundry ajoute son propre garde-fou quand un chat lié travaille depuis l'écran Knowledge Base dans l'application : connected-browser-run.ts demande une approbation pour chaque écriture cloud et ne propose pas d'autorisation valable pour toute la session. Si tu le mets en place toi-même Mets une version dans la citation, pas seulement un ID. Utilise la même valeur que ton outil de modification accepte comme expected_version , pour qu'une seule lecture te donne les deux. Tiens un journal d'événements par base de connaissances avec une séquence monotone, et laisse l'agent reprendre à partir d'un numéro. Un entier d'état côté client remplace la relecture de tout ce qu'il a jamais cité. Réponds uniquement à partir de contenu publié et journalise la dépublication comme un événement, pour qu'une citation puisse revenir comme "disparue" et pas seulement comme "différente". Fais des modifications un compare-and-swap sur le contenu complet avec une clé d'idempotence obligatoire. Dis au modèle, dans la description de l'outil, de relire avant de modifier, car une version tirée d'une citation vieille d'une heure échoue environ quatre fois sur dix. Marque l'outil d'écriture comme destructive et open-world, et garde aussi de ton côté une approbation par appel. Ce qu'osFoundry entend par retrieval et grounding se trouve dans son entrée de glossaire sur le RAG . L'organisation de ses bases de connaissances est décrite sur la page des bases de connaissances .

title: Regenerate Only What Moved: An Anchor Manifest for Model-Drafted Docs
author: Avery Lin
summary: Most documentation pipelines that use a model regenerate the whole page, and that is where both the risk and the cost live. A page is a bundle of claims with different owners, different evidence, and very different lifetimes. Regenerating a page to fix one stale paragraph quietly rewrites five paragraphs that were already correct and already approved. The fix is structural: bind every claim to the code that justifies it, then regenerate only the claims whose evidence actually moved. The workflow below is small enough to adopt in an afternoon and specific enough to argue with. It has an anchor manifest, a four-state drift plan, a drafting step where a model is allowed to write, and a review queue where it is not. Every number this workflow reports comes from your own repository, which is the only honest source of such numbers. The failure mode, stated precisely A diff of a regenerated page mixes three kinds of change, and reviewers cannot separate them from the rendered result. Some changes are real drift caused by a code change, some are sampling noise from the model, and some are the model's editorial taste applied to prose that was fine. Under a whole-page pipeline these three arrive in one lump, so the reviewer either approves all of it or abandons the diff. The second problem is cost asymmetry. A page with fourteen claims usually has one or two that are stale, so you spend model calls and human attention on twelve claims with nothing wrong with them. Repeated often enough, that pattern teaches reviewers to rubber-stamp, which is the worst outcome a documentation review process can produce. The manifest approach removes both problems by making regeneration a targeted operation instead of a bulk one. You first prove which claims drifted, then you spend model time only there, and the reviewer sees a short, explainable queue instead of a page-sized diff. Step 1: Anchor one claim per code reference An anchor is an HTML comment on the line immediately above a claim, and it names the code location that would make the claim false if it changed. Keep the granularity tight; one anchor covers exactly one claim, never a section. ## Retry behavior <!-- anchor: src/limiter/backoff.py#compute_backoff --> Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and stop at the configured cap. <!-- /anchor --> <!-- anchor: src/limiter/backoff.py#MAX_ATTEMPTS --> The limiter allows `MAX_ATTEMPTS` attempts per request. <!-- /anchor --> The reference format is path#symbol , where the symbol is a function, a class, or a module-level constant. Claims with no defensible anchor are still allowed, but they are invisible to this pipeline and must be owned by a human explicitly. That gap is a feature: it forces you to notice which sentences no code can support. Step 2: Build the manifest and classify drift The script below parses anchored claims, resolves each anchor to a fingerprint, and compares that fingerprint against a committed manifest. Fingerprints hash the symbol body with per-line whitespace stripped, so a reformat or a reindent does not fake a drift event. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ anchordoc.py - plan documentation regeneration from code anchors. Usage: python anchordoc.py plan --docs docs/ --manifest docs.anchors.json python anchordoc.py accept --docs docs/ --manifest docs.anchors.json --owner avery """ from __future__ import annotations import argparse , hashlib , json , re , subprocess from datetime import datetime , timezone from pathlib import Path ANCHOR_RE = re . compile ( r " <!--\s*anchor:\s*(?P<ref>[^\s>]+)\s*--> " ) DEF_RE = re . compile ( r " ^(?P<indent>\s*)(?:(?:async\s+)?def|class)\s+(?P<fn>\w+) " r " |^(?P<const>[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*)\s*= " ) def git_blob ( path : Path ) -> str : out = subprocess . run ([ " git " , " hash-object " , str ( path )], capture_output = True , text = True , check = True ) return out . stdout . strip () def symbol_fingerprint ( path : Path , symbol : str ) -> str | None : lines = path . read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ). splitlines () for i , line in enumerate ( lines ): m = DEF_RE . match ( line ) if not m or ( m . group ( " fn " ) or m . group ( " const " )) != symbol : continue body = [ line ] if m . group ( " fn " ): # block ends at first dedent indent = len ( m . group ( " indent " )) for nxt in lines [ i + 1 :]: if nxt . strip () and len ( nxt ) - len ( nxt . lstrip ()) <= indent : break body . append ( nxt ) norm = " \n " . join ( b . strip () for b in body if b . strip ()) return hashlib . sha256 ( norm . encode ()). hexdigest ()[: 16 ] return None def parse_claims ( doc : Path ) -> list [ dict ]: text = doc . read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " ) claims , cursor = [], 0 for m in ANCHOR_RE . finditer ( text ): if claims : claims [ - 1 ][ " text " ] = text [ claims [ - 1 ][ " start " ]: m . start ()]. strip () claims . append ({ " anchor " : m . group ( " ref " ), " start " : m . end ()}) if claims : claims [ - 1 ][ " text " ] = text [ claims [ - ArgumentParser () ap . add_argument ( " mode " , choices = [ " plan " , " accept " ]) ap . add_argument ( " --docs " , required = True , type = Path ) ap . add_argument ( " --manifest " , required = True , type = Path ) ap . add_argument ( " --owner " , default = " unassigned " ) args = ap . parse_args () manifest = json . loads ( args . manifest . read_text ()) if args . manifest . exists () else {} repo = Path . cwd () plan = { " fresh " : [], " stale " : [], " orphan " : [], " new " : []} for doc in sorted ( args . docs . rglob ( " *.md " )): for claim in parse_claims ( doc ): key = f " { doc . as_posix () } | { claim [ ' anchor ' ] } " fp = resolve ( claim [ " anchor " ], repo ) if fp is None : plan [ " orphan " ]. append ({ " key " : key , " anchor " : claim [ " anchor " ]}) continue entry = manifest . get ( key ) if entry is None : plan [ " new " ]. append ({ " key " : key , " fingerprint " : fp }) elif entry [ " fingerprint " ] != fp : plan [ " stale " ]. append ({ " key " : key , " was " : entry [ " fingerprint " ], " now " : fp , " class " : entry . get ( " class " )}) else : plan [ " fresh " ]. append ({ " key " : key }) if args . mode == " accept " : manifest [ key ] = { " fingerprint " : fp , " owner " : args . owner , " class " : entry . get ( " class " ) if entry else " behavior " , " approved_at " : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) . strftime ( " %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ " )} if args . mode == " accept " : args . manifest . write_text ( json . dumps ( manifest , indent = 2 , sort_keys = True ) + " \n " ) print ( f " accepted { len ( manifest ) } claims into { args . manifest } " ) else : plan [ " counts " ] = { k : len ( v ) for k , v in plan . items ()} print ( json . dumps ( plan , indent = 2 )) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () This is a reference implementation, not a blessed one; run it on a scratch branch before you trust its plan output. The two commands that matter are the plan run and the human-only accept run. python tools/anchordoc.py plan --docs docs/ --manifest docs.anchors.json > regenerations.json python tools/anchordoc.py accept --docs docs/ --manifest docs.anchors.json --owner avery A plan output has a predictable shape, and the counts line is the one you read first. If stale is consistently a small fraction of fresh , your anchors are doing their job and your regeneration budget is small. { "fresh" : [{ "key" : "docs/retries.md|src/limiter/backoff.py#compute_backoff" }], "stale" : [{ "key" : "docs/retries.md|src/limiter/backoff.py#MAX_ATTEMPTS" , "was" : "3b91c0d7a2e4f1aa" , "now" : "9f2c1ab34d5e6f70" , "class" : "behavior" }], "orphan" : [{ "key" : "docs/limits.md|src/limiter/budget.py#spend" , "anchor" : "src/limiter/budget.py#spend" }], "new" : [{ "key" : "docs/limits.md|src/limiter/budget.py#reset" , "fingerprint" : "77aa1c90d2be4410" }], "counts" : { "fresh" : 41 , "stale" : 2 , "orphan" : 1 , "new" : 0 } } Step 3: Read the four states as four different jobs Drift is not one condition, and collapsing the states is how teams end up regenerating things that were never broken. Treat each state as a distinct task with a distinct owner. State Meaning Next action Who acts fresh Fingerprint matches the approved manifest Do nothing; do not send it to a model Nobody stale Source symbol changed since approval Draft a replacement, then route by claim class Model drafts, human signs orphan Anchor no longer resolves Fix the manifest or the claim by hand Human new Anchored claim with no approved baseline Review the text once, then accept it Human The most important row is fresh , because the correct action there is inaction. Any pipeline that touches fresh claims has already given up the main benefit of this design. Orphans deserve a second look as well: a rename looks exactly like a deletion, so a two-line manifest edit is usually the whole fix. Step 4: Draft only the stale claims Now the model gets a narrow job with real evidence attached: one claim, one symbol body, and an instruction to prefer silence over invention. The drafting step writes to a separate directory and never overwrites the approved document. This is where a free model tier becomes genuinely useful, because the calls are small, scoped, and easy to discard. I use MonkeyCode's free model access for exactly this step; the drafting call stays a thin wrapper so the endpoint can be swapped without touching the plan logic. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. jq -r '.stale[] | [.key, .class] | @tsv' regenerations.json \ | while IFS = $' \t ' read -r key class ; do python tools/draft_claim.py --key " $key " --class " $class " \ --out "docs/drafts/ $( echo " $key " | cut -d '|' -f1 | xargs basename ) " done The prompt skeleton matters more than the transport, and the escape hatch on the last line is deliberate. A model that is allowed to answer UNCHANGED stops inventing filler after a refactor that did not change behavior. You may rewrite only the claim text below, using the source as ground truth. Do not introduce numbers, dates, version strings, guarantees, or new capabilities. Return exactly one paragraph of prose, or the token UNCHANGED. CLAIM: {claim_text} SOURCE: {symbol_body} Step 5: Route drafts by claim class, not by confidence A model's self-reported confidence is not a routing signal, but the class of claim is. The table below is the part of this workflow I would defend hardest, because it encodes who can be blamed when a sentence is wrong. Claim class Example Model may draft? Human must own Behavior narrative "Retries back off exponentially until the cap" Yes, when stale Doc owner confirms the code path Numeric limits and timeouts "The cap is 30 seconds" Yes, but the number must be grepped from source Reviewer verifies the value in the diff Versions and deprecation dates "Removed in 3.0" No Release owner Security, privacy, licensing "Tokens are never logged" No Named role, not the doc owner Setup and migration commands make migrate-dry-run Yes Someone runs every command before merge API signatures Function parameters and types No, generate from introspection Tooling, then a spot check Intent and roadmap "We plan to consolidate this" No anchor can support it Product owner, outside this pipeline The numeric row is the subtle one: the model may write the sentence, but the number has to come from the source, not from the model's summary of it. The intent row explains why some paragraphs must be marked as unanchored on purpose, rather than given a plausible anchor that no code can justify. Step 6: Schedule the planning run, not the drafting run Running the planner on a schedule is cheap and safe, because it only reads code and writes a JSON plan. The drafting loop should stay manual until your approval rate stabilizes, since a scheduled drafting loop mostly produces orphan drafts nobody reads. A free server option is a reasonable home for the planning job, since the work is a short weekly read over a checkout. Treat that availability as convenience rather than a dependency, and keep the job off your release critical path entirely. # weekly, 07:00 UTC - plan only, no writes to docs/ 0 7 * * 1 cd /srv/repo && git pull --ff-only && \ python tools/anchordoc.py plan --docs docs/ --manifest docs.anchors.json \ > reports/regen- $( date +%F ) .json What to measure every week Three numbers tell you whether the workflow is working, and all three come straight out of the plan output. Stale ratio is stale / (stale + fresh) ; orphan count is the number of anchors that no longer resolve; median staleness age is how long stale claims waited for an owner. Add one process number on top: regeneration precision, the share of model drafts a reviewer accepted without substantive edits. If precision drops while the stale ratio holds steady, your drafting step is the problem, not your anchors. If the orphan count grows every week, your anchors are too fine-grained for the refactor rate of the code they track. Neither signal requires a new tool; both require a decision about claim granularity. Limitations and who should skip this The fingerprint detects change, not meaning, so a comment-only commit or a pure rename-preparation refactor can flip a claim to stale with no semantic drift. Expect false positives and budget a few minutes per week to dismiss them. The symbol extraction here is Python-shaped and will miss decorators with multi-line bodies, dynamically created methods, and most non-Python languages without a rewrite. A fresh fingerprint is not a correctness guarantee, and this is the limitation that matters most. A sentence that was wrong when it was accepted stays wrong forever if the code behind it never changes, which is why the new state needs a real human read rather than a rubber stamp. Skip this workflow if your claims live outside the repository, such as pricing pages, SLAs, or anything legal reviews. Skip it if you have no git-tracked version of record, since the manifest is meaningless without one. Skip it as well if nobody can spare a reviewer for the human queue, because this design trades model time for human attention rather than the reverse. If your docs already live beside your code, the manifest is a one-time afternoon of annotation and a weekly read afterwards. Start with the behavior class only, measure regeneration precision for two weeks, and widen the scope only when reviewers stop rewriting the drafts.

title: Auditar un modelo de 180B sin descargarlo: leer cabeceras safetensors por HTTP Range con Python
author: 김민식/학생
summary: TL;DR Antes de reservar 8 GPU o de bajar 360 GB, puedes auditar un checkpoint de Hugging Face leyendo solo las cabeceras de sus archivos safetensors . Lo hice con Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 (un MoE de 512 expertos, FINAL-Bench/Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 ): 131 shards, 262 peticiones HTTP Range y 229.760 bytes leídos (224 KiB, unas 1,57 millones de veces menos que los 360 GB del modelo). Con eso comprobé que los 131 shards tienen el tamaño que declara su cabecera, que los 1.658 tensores del índice coinciden uno a uno con los de las cabeceras y que el total es 179.999.981.459 parámetros, el mismo número que publica la API de Hugging Face. Además salen tres datos de diseño útiles: el 67,1 % de los parámetros son expertos enrutados, el 28,8 % son tablas de embeddings (n-gram) que no se multiplican enteras en cada token, y la caché K/V a 262.144 tokens ocupa 6,0 GiB por secuencia porque solo 12 de las 48 capas usan atención completa. Abajo está el script completo y una calculadora de memoria. Aviso de entrada: este es un modelo de VIDRAFT y esta cuenta es de VIDRAFT. Todo lo que mido son archivos públicos del repositorio, y cualquiera puede repetir el análisis con el código de este artículo. ¿Por qué auditar un checkpoint antes de descargarlo? Un modelo de 180B en BF16 pesa 360,0 GB (335,3 GiB) repartidos en 131 archivos. Si te equivocas al planificar, lo descubres después de horas de descarga o, peor, cuando vllm serve se queda sin memoria. Con unos pocos kilobytes de metadatos respondes de antemano tres preguntas de ingeniería: ¿Está completo y es coherente? (tamaños, offsets, índice) ¿Dónde están los parámetros? (expertos, atención, embeddings) ¿Cabe en mi hardware, y con cuánto contexto? ¿Cómo se leen las cabeceras safetensors sin bajar los pesos? El formato safetensors es deliberadamente simple: los primeros 8 bytes son un entero u64 little-endian con el largo n de una cabecera JSON; después vienen n bytes de JSON con, por cada tensor, su dtype , su shape y su data_offsets (inicio y fin dentro de la zona de datos). Los pesos van a continuación. Como Hugging Face sirve los archivos con soporte de Range , basta con pedir bytes=0-7 y luego bytes=8-(8+n-1) . Este es el script completo que ejecuté (solo biblioteca estándar de Python): import json , struct , urllib . request from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor from math import prod REPO = " FINAL-Bench/Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 " BASE = f " https://huggingface.co/ { REPO } /resolve/main/ " def get ( archivo , a = None , b = None ): req = urllib . request . Request ( BASE + archivo , headers = { " User-Agent " : " auditor/1.0 " }) if a is not None : req . add_header ( " Range " , f " bytes= { a } - { b } " ) return urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = 60 ). read () def cabecera ( shard ): n = struct . unpack ( " <Q " , get ( shard , 0 , 7 ))[ 0 ] # 8 bytes: largo del JSON h = json . loads ( get ( shard , 8 , 8 + n - 1 )) # solo el JSON, no los pesos h . pop ( " __metadata__ " , None ) return h indice = json . loads ( get ( " model.safetensors.index.json " ))[ " weight_map " ] shards = sorted ( set ( indice . values ())) with ThreadPoolExecutor ( 8 ) as ex : cabeceras = list ( ex . map ( cabecera , shards )) def tipo ( nombre ): if " visual " in nombre : return " vision " if " mtp " in nombre : return " mtp " if " ngram_embedding " in nombre or " embed_tokens " in nombre : return " embeddings " if " shared_expert " in nombre : return " experto_compartido " if " experts " in nombre : return " expertos " if " linear_attn " in nombre : return " atencion_lineal " if " .self_attn. " in nombre : return " atencion_completa " if nombre . startswith ( " lm_head " ): return " lm_head " return " otros " por_tipo = {} for h in cabeceras : for nombre , t in h . items (): por_tipo [ tipo ( nombre )] = por_tipo . get ( tipo ( nombre ), 0 ) + prod ( t [ " shape " ]) total = sum ( por_tipo . values ()) for k , v in sorted ( por_tipo . items (), key = lambda kv : - kv [ 1 ]): print ( f " { k : 20 s } { v : > 16 , d } { 100 * v / total : 6.2 f } % " ) print ( f " { ' TOTAL ' : 20 s } { total : > 16 , d } " ) La salida real, medida hoy sobre el repositorio público: Categoría Parámetros % del total Expertos enrutados 120.795.955.200 67,11 % Embeddings (tablas n-gram + embed_tokens ) 51.835.944.960 28,80 % Capa MTP 2.607.150.848 1,45 % Atención lineal 2.086.510.464 1,16 % Otros (normas, routers, mezcla) 736.378.915 0,41 % lm_head 635.699.200 0,35 % Atención completa 617.358.336 0,34 % Visión 448.931.056 0,25 % Experto compartido 236.052.480 0,13 % Total 179.999.981.459 100 % La suma coincide al parámetro con el campo safetensors.total de la API de Hugging Face (179.999.981.459, de los cuales 179.999.981.424 son BF16 y 35 son enteros I64). Esa coincidencia es la primera señal de que las cabeceras y el resumen de la plataforma cuentan la misma historia. ¿Qué comprobaciones de integridad se pueden hacer solo con cabeceras? Cuatro, todas sin descargar un solo peso: Comprobación Resultado en R3 Tamaño del archivo = 8 + n + mayor data_offsets[1] 131 de 131 shards Huecos entre tensores consecutivos dentro de un shard 0 Nombres en model.safetensors.index.json frente a nombres en cabeceras 1.658 y 1.658, conjuntos idénticos Tensores cuyo shard en el índice difiere del shard real 0 La primera es la más útil para detectar descargas truncadas o subidas incompletas: si el archivo tiene menos bytes que los que anuncia su cabecera, el shard está cortado. Para obtener el tamaño remoto usa GET /api/models/<repo>?blobs=true , que devuelve size y lfs.sha256 por archivo. Las cabeceras no demuestran que el contenido sea el correcto, solo que es estructuralmente consistente. Para el contenido existe el hash. Como prueba, bajé el shard más pequeño ( model-00001-of-00131.safetensors , 1.040.155.944 bytes), calculé su SHA-256 en streaming y lo comparé con el lfs.sha256 de la API: coincide ( db4dbc41ff71... ). Si vas a descargar los 131, haz esa misma comparación shard por shard; es una sola línea con hashlib . ¿Dónde están los 180B parámetros de un MoE de 512 expertos? Los números de arriba tienen una lectura directa. Cada capa tiene un tensor fusionado experts.gate_up_proj de forma [512, 1280, 2560] y un experts.down_proj de forma [512, 2560, 640] . Con 48 capas salen 120.795.955.200 parámetros, es decir, 2.516.582.400 por capa y 4.915.200 por experto (3 x 2560 x 640). El router elige 10 de los 512 expertos por token. El segundo bloque llama la atención: 51,8 mil millones de parámetros, el 28,8 %, no son capas de cómputo. Son 128 tablas ngram_embedding de forma [2.500.012, 160] (51.200.245.760 parámetros, el 28,4 % del total) más el embedding de tokens. Por su forma y su nombre son tablas de consulta por fila: un token lee unas pocas filas, no multiplica la tabla entera. Para quien planifica memoria esto importa: esos 103,7 GB en BF16 tienen que estar residentes, pero no consumen ancho de banda en cada paso de decodificación como lo haría una capa densa del mismo tamaño. ¿Cuántos parámetros trabajan realmente en cada token? La ficha del modelo indica 10 expertos activos por token, pero no publica una cifra de parámetros activos. Con los tamaños de tensor puedo estimarla (es mi cálculo, no una cifra oficial): expertos_activos = 120_795_955_200 * 10 / 512 # 2.359.296.000 con_computo = ( expertos_activos + 617_358_336 # atención completa + 2_086_510_464 # atención lineal + 236_052_480 # experto compartido + 635_699_200 # lm_head + 736_378_915 ) # otros print ( f " { con_computo : ,. 0 f } ( { 100 * con_computo / 179_999_981_459 : . 2 f } % del total) " ) # salida: 6,671,295,395 (3.71 % del total) Son unos 6,67 mil millones de parámetros con cómputo por token en la ruta de texto (sin la capa MTP ni la visión), un 3,7 % del total. Para un decodificador de una sola secuencia, el límite superior de velocidad lo da el ancho de banda de memoria dividido por los bytes que se leen por token: Precisión GB leídos por token Límite con 100 GB/s Límite con 400 GB/s BF16 13,3 7,5 tok/s 30,0 tok/s ~4,5 bits por peso 3,75 26,6 tok/s 106,6 tok/s Son cotas teóricas ilustrativas (ignoran la lectura de las tablas de embeddings, el solapamiento de expertos entre tokens, la activación y la sobrecarga del motor). La ficha del modelo reporta, para el GGUF de 4 bits de 111 GB (POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF), entre 18 y 21 tok/s solo con CPU: es una cifra de la ficha, que no medí aquí, y cae dentro de la cota de 26,6 tok/s que sale de esta cuenta con 100 GB/s. ¿Cuánta memoria de caché K/V necesita un contexto de 262.144 tokens? Aquí el diseño híbrido marca la diferencia. En config.json , layer_types alterna tres capas linear_attention con una full_attention ( full_attention_interval = 4 ), así que solo 12 de las 48 capas guardan K/V que crece con el contexto. Con num_key_value_heads = 2 , head_dim = 256 y BF16: capas_completas , kv_heads , head_dim , bytes_ = 12 , 2 , 256 , 2 por_token = capas_completas * 2 * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_ # K y V print ( por_token , por_token * 262_144 / 2 ** 30 ) # salida: 24576 6.0 (bytes por token, GiB por secuencia) Son 24 KiB por token y 6,0 GiB por secuencia de 262.144 tokens. Si las 48 capas usaran atención completa serían 24 GiB. Las 36 capas de atención lineal guardan un estado de tamaño fijo. Suponiendo el diseño habitual [cabezas de valor, dim clave, dim valor] en float32 (48 x 128 x 128 x 4 bytes = 3,1 MB por capa, más un estado de convolución de 61 KB), son unos 115 MB por secuencia, independientes de la longitud. Esa suposición del layout del estado es mía; el resultado cambia poco el total porque el término dominante es el K/V de las 12 capas completas. Esta cuenta no incluye el índice de atención dispersa ( indexer_* ) ni la capa MTP, así que trátala como el K/V principal, no como el total exacto de un motor concreto. ¿Cabe en mi GPU? Una calculadora de memoria Con los pesos (359.999.962.918 bytes según model.safetensors.index.json ) y el coste por secuencia (6,56 GB entre K/V y estados) se arma una calculadora corta: def secuencias_completas ( n_gpu , gb_por_gpu , uso = 0.90 , pesos_gb = 360.0 , seq_gb = 6.558 ): libre = n_gpu * gb_por_gpu * uso - pesos_gb return max ( 0 , int ( libre // seq_gb )) for nombre , n , gb in [( " 8xH100 " , 8 , 80 ), ( " 4xH200 " , 4 , 141 ), ( " 4xB200 " , 4 , 192 ), ( " 2xB200 " , 2 , 192 )]: print ( nombre , secuencias_completas ( n , gb )) Configuración Memoria utilizable (90 %) Tras cargar los pesos Secuencias de 262k 8 x H100 80 GB 576,0 GB 216,0 GB 32 4 x H200 141 GB 507,6 GB 147,6 GB 22 4 x B200 192 GB 691,2 GB 331,2 GB 50 2 x B200 192 GB 345,6 GB no caben los pesos en BF16 0 Esto es una estimación de planificación: descuenta pesos, K/V y estados, y deja el 10 % restante para activaciones, grafos CUDA y fragmentación. La receta de la ficha usa --tensor-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel , que corresponde a la primera fila. Para menos memoria, la ficha enlaza la versión GGUF de 4 bits (111 GB) en lugar de BF16. Alcance de las cifras Todo el análisis sale de metadatos públicos y de un hash comprobado, medido el 2026-11-09. No ejecuté inferencia, así que no hay aquí ningún dato de calidad ni de velocidad medida; las velocidades son cotas teóricas y la cifra de la ficha se atribuye a la ficha. La clasificación de tensores por nombre es una heurística mía (los nombres siguen la convención del repositorio) y la cuadratura exacta con el total de la API la respalda. Lo que sí puedes hacer es repetir el script y obtener los mismos números. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Puedo leer las cabeceras safetensors sin descargar el archivo completo? Sí. Pide bytes=0-7 para obtener el largo n de la cabecera y luego bytes=8-(8+n-1) para leer el JSON. En este modelo, las 131 cabeceras suman 229.760 bytes. ¿Qué diferencia hay entre parámetros totales y parámetros activos en un MoE? El total cuenta todos los expertos (aquí 512 por capa); el activo cuenta los que procesan cada token (aquí 10 por capa, más la atención y el experto compartido). Por la forma de los tensores, en R3 son unos 6,67 mil millones de parámetros con cómputo por token, frente a 180 mil millones almacenados. ¿Cómo detecto una descarga truncada? Compara 8 + n + max(data_offsets[1]) con el tamaño del archivo. Si no coinciden, el shard está incompleto. Después verifica el SHA-256 con el valor lfs.sha256 de la API. ¿Por qué la caché K/V es tan pequeña a 262k tokens? Porque solo 12 de las 48 capas son de atención completa; las otras 36 son de atención lineal con estado fijo. Resultado: 24 KiB por token y 6,0 GiB por secuencia, frente a 24 GiB si todas las capas fueran de atención completa. ¿Sirve este método para otros modelos de Hugging Face? Sí, para cualquier repositorio con safetensors . Solo cambian el nombre del repo y, si quieres clasificar parámetros, las reglas de tipo() según la arquitectura. title: osFoundry는 왜 Codex에게 핸드오프 제안과 run 요청을 다른 툴로 줄까
author: BBT
summary: osFoundry MCP 서버에 로그인 전 Codex CLI가 세션 툴을 처음 호출하면 이렇게 돌아온다. POST /api/v1/external-mcp {"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"propose_session_handoff","arguments":{}}} HTTP / 2 401 www-authenticate : Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.osfoundry.io/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/v1/external-mcp", error="invalid_token", error_description="Connect osFoundry to continue" {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"isError":true, "content":[{"type":"text","text":"Authentication required"}], …}} initialize 랑 tools/list 는 토큰 없이도 답한다. 그래서 클라이언트는 아무도 로그인하지 않은 상태에서 툴 59개를 다 볼 수 있다. 그중에 같은 일을 하는 것처럼 보이는 두 개가 있다. { "name" : "propose_session_handoff" , "description" : "Send a scoped task and context summary to the owner of an invited session. The owner must accept before a run is queued." , "required" : [ "session_type" , "session_id" , "goal" , "context_summary" , "requested_output" , "idempotency_key" ], "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : false , "openWorldHint" : true , "destructiveHint" : true }, "securitySchemes" : [{ "type" : "oauth2" , "scopes" : [ "osfoundry:write" ]}]} { "name" : "request_session_run" , "description" : "Queue a bounded goal for an agent, team, or loop session where this assistant is an invited runner. The osFoundry runtime executes the task when available." , "required" : [ "session_type" , "session_id" , "goal" , "idempotency_key" ], "annotations" : { "readOnlyHint" : false , "openWorldHint" : false , "destructiveHint" : true }, "securitySchemes" : [{ "type" : "oauth2" , "scopes" : [ "osfoundry:run" ]}]} 둘 다 결국 세션이 일을 하게 만든다. 이 글에서는 왜 하나로 안 합쳤는지, 각각 어떤 제한이 걸려 있는지 보고, 클라이언트 쪽을 Python으로 다시 만들어서 그 제한을 라이브 스키마에 직접 대 봤다. 두 호출을 가르는 건 뭘까 누가, 언제 OK를 하느냐다. 핸드오프는 그 자리에서 사람한테 묻는다. 오너한테 "Codex CLI requests a handoff" 알림이 가고, 세션의 Handoffs 탭 "Outside assistant requests"에 올라온다. 보이는 건 goal, 접혀 있는 "Context and expected output", 그리고 "Up to N rounds on your agent runtime" 한 줄이다. 누가 Accept and run을 누르기 전까지 큐에는 아무것도 안 들어간다. 웹 클라이언트는 /agent-sessions/{id}/external-handoffs/{handoff_id}/decision 에 {decision: "accept"} 를 POST하고, 토스트로 "Handoff accepted and run queued"가 뜬다. 핸드오프 행은 pending 에서 accepted , declined , cancelled 중 하나로 넘어간다. run은 승인이 이미 끝나 있다. 오너가 Connected 탭에서 연결에 Runner 자리를 준 순간이 OK다. 거기 설명문은 이렇다. "Invite it to a session as Contributor to post notes and propose handoffs, or Runner to also request runs. A handoff still needs the session owner's approval." 로그인 화면에서도 run 스코프는 "Run sessions where you grant a runner role"로 나온다. needs_approval 플래그 하나 달린 툴로 합쳤다면, 사람한테 물을지 말지를 호출하는 쪽이 정하게 된다. 툴을 둘로 쪼개면 그 결정이 오너 쪽, 그것도 호출자가 손댈 수 없는 두 군데로 간다. OAuth 스코프( osfoundry:write 냐 osfoundry:run 이냐)와 자리(Contributor냐 Runner냐)다. Codex 설정의 scopes 에서 osfoundry:run 을 빼 두면 Runner 자리가 있어도 run을 못 띄운다. 어노테이션도 같은 선으로 갈린다. propose_session_handoff 는 결과가 호출 밖의 사람한테 닿으니까 openWorldHint: true . request_session_run 은 미리 동의한 세션의 큐만 건드리니까 openWorldHint: false . 둘 다 destructiveHint: true 라서 Codex를 default_tools_approval_mode = "writes" 로 돌리면 둘 다 실행 전에 확인을 받는다. 핸드오프만 컨텍스트 요약이 필수인 이유 뭔가 돌기 전에 사람이 읽기 때문이다. context_summary 와 requested_output 은 핸드오프에선 필수고 run에는 아예 없다. 오너는 자기 세션 런타임을 여기에 쓸지 말지 정해야 하는데, "export 고쳐줘"만으로는 못 정한다. Runner는 그 신뢰를 이미 받았으니 run은 goal 만 받는다. 길이 제한도 다르다. 핸드오프의 goal 은 5,000자, 컨텍스트 5,000자, 원하는 결과물 1,000자까지. run의 goal 은 10,000자까지 된다. run엔 다른 칸이 없으니 실제로는 goal 에 컨텍스트까지 같이 쓰게 된다. Codex는 뭘 다시 읽을 수 있나 세션이 가진 것보다 적다. read_session_task_result : "the status and attributed runtime result for one task started by this connection". 다른 연결의 task id를 넣어도 소용없다. read_session_mail : "notes addressed to this connection and notes it posted". 페이지당 1~20개, 오래된 건 before_id 로 넘긴다. "Internal agent analysis is excluded." read_session_state : 참여한 세션의 현재 상태와 최근 태스크. post_session_note : 이름이 붙은 노트를 남긴다. 에이전트는 "the returned external sender slug"로 답장할 수 있다. "does not trigger an automatic run"이라서 노트로 오너의 클릭을 우회할 수는 없다. 팀 세션에서는 이 노트가 Team mail에 연결의 표시 이름과 "outside assistant" 라벨을 달고 올라온다. 다시 만들어 보기 이 Mac엔 codex 바이너리가 없어서 handoff_sim.py (약 220줄)가 클라이언트 역할을 한다. 하는 일은 세 가지다. 토큰 없이 라이브 서버에 initialize , tools/list , tools/call 을 각각 15번 보내고 툴 목록을 저장한다. 인자 케이스 12개를 라이브 inputSchema 에 jsonschema (Draft 2020-12)로 검증한다. 제한값은 추측하지 않는다. 자리, 스코프, 오너의 결정, 멱등성을 작은 인메모리 모델로 돌린다. osFoundry 서버 코드는 공개돼 있지 않아서, 이 부분은 툴 설명과 핸드오프를 보여 주는 웹 클라이언트를 보고 재구성한 거다. 응답은 모델의 것이지 서버의 것이 아니다. $ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 handoff_sim.py 와이어 initialize HTTP 200 median 566.3 p90 799.0 tools/list HTTP 200 median 559.7 p90 937.7 tools/call (no token) HTTP 401 median 482.6 p90 677.0 단위는 밀리초. 일본에 있는 이 Mac에서 CloudFront KIX 엣지를 거쳐 잰 거라 서버보다는 경로 숫자에 가깝다. 볼 건 모양이다. 툴 탐색은 공짜고 Codex 켤 때마다 돌려도 부담이 없다. 첫 진짜 호출은 401 왕복 한 번이 들고, 그 401이 resource_metadata 를 실어 온다. Codex는 따로 알려 주지 않아도 이걸로 OAuth 서버를 찾는다. 세션 툴 7개는 전체 목록 10,197토큰 중 1,152토큰(11.3%)이었다. cl100k_base 로 센 거라 Codex 토크나이저 기준으로는 대략적인 값이다. enabled_tools 에 이 7개만 넣으면 프롬프트가 작아진다. 제한값 툴 스코프 필수 제한 propose_session_handoff write 6 goal 5,000, context 5,000, output 1,000, max_rounds 1–10 cancel_session_handoff write 1 handoff_id만 request_session_run run 4 goal 10,000, max_rounds 1–10 read_session_state read 2 없음 read_session_task_result read 3 없음 read_session_mail read 2 limit 1–20 post_session_note write 5 subject 200, body 10,000 라이브 스키마에 12케이스를 대 본 결과다. propose_session_handoff 6,000-char goal REJECT maxLength: goal request_session_run 6,000-char goal ok propose_session_handoff no context_summary REJECT required propose_session_handoff max_rounds omitted ok request_session_run max_rounds 0 REJECT minimum: max_rounds request_session_run max_rounds 11 REJECT maximum: max_rounds request_session_run no idempotency_key REJECT required request_session_run session_type 'room' REJECT enum: session_type request_session_run extra field 'model' REJECT additionalProperties read_session_mail limit 21 REJECT maximum: limit post_session_note 201-char subject REJECT maxLength: subject cancel_session_handoff only handoff_id ok 두 개는 다시 볼 만하다. 같은 6,000자 goal이 run에선 통과하고 핸드오프에선 너무 길다. 긴 프롬프트 하나 만들어서 쓸 수 있는 툴에 아무거나 던지는 클라이언트는 여기서 삽질한다. 그리고 additionalProperties: false 가 model 필드를 막는다. 호출자는 세션 모델을 고를 수 없고, 세션은 자기 설정대로 돈다. max_rounds 는 둘 다 생략할 수 있다. 기본값이 스키마에 안 나와 있으니 횟수가 중요하면 명시해서 보내는 게 낫다. 자리, 취소, 승인 (모델) tool observer contributor runner propose_session_handoff - yes yes cancel_session_handoff - yes yes request_session_run - - yes read_session_state yes yes yes read_session_task_result yes yes yes read_session_mail yes yes yes post_session_note - yes yes runner seat, token without osfoundry:run -> {'error': 'token lacks osfoundry:run'} cancel while pending -> {'status': 'cancelled'} owner clicks Accept after cancel -> cancelled owner accepts -> accepted | cancel after -> {'error': 'already accepted'} another connection reads that task -> {'error': 'not a task started by this connection'} 표는 Connected 탭 설명문을 그대로 표로 옮긴 거다. 재밌는 건 취소 창이다. cancel_session_handoff 는 "before its owner accepts it"에만 먹히니까, 먼저 일어난 쪽이 이긴다. run이 큐에 들어간 뒤엔 거두는 게 더 이상 호출자 몫이 아니다. 취소가 handoff_id 만 받는 것도 그래서다. 넘길 상태가 없고, 닫을 건 대기 중인 행 하나뿐이다. 응답이 사라질 때 쓰기 툴은 전부 idempotency_key 가 필수다. 이게 뭘 막는지 보려고 모델에서 request_session_run 을 1,000번 보내고, 응답의 20%를 버리고(seed 7), 클라이언트가 같은 키로 최대 3번 재시도하게 했다. server honours idempotency_key=True calls sent 1276 tasks queued 1000 duplicates 0 server honours idempotency_key=False calls sent 1276 tasks queued 1276 duplicates 276 남의 런타임에서 run이 276번 더 도는 거다. 필수 키는 바로 이 경우 때문에 있다. 타임아웃 나서 재시도하는 클라이언트라면 누구나 밟을 수 있고, 이미 시작된 run은 두 번 필요 없다. 선택이 아니라 필수라서 빼먹는 클라이언트가 나올 수 없다. 스크립트 전체는 Apple M1에서 실시간 26.4초 걸렸다. 거의 다 네트워크 호출 45번이고 user CPU 시간은 0.37초였다. 직접 붙인다면 "사람한테 묻기"와 "미리 받은 허락으로 움직이기"를 스코프가 다른 두 툴로 나눈다. 오너의 선택은 호출자가 정하는 인자가 아니라 토큰과 자리에 둔다. 사람이 판단할 때 쓰는 필드( context_summary , requested_output )는 제안 쪽에만 필수로 두고, run의 goal보다 제한을 빡빡하게 잡는다. 호출자가 취소할 수 있는 건 대기 중일 때뿐이다. 승인 후에 멈추는 건 오너 일이다. 다시 읽기는 그 연결이 시작한 것, 그 연결 앞으로 온 것으로 좁힌다. 세션 내부 분석은 빼 둔다. 쓰기는 전부 idempotency_key 필수로 하고, 중복이면 첫 결과를 돌려준다. 스키마는 additionalProperties: false 로 닫아서, 세션이 고르지 않은 모델이나 툴 목록을 호출자가 끼워 넣지 못하게 한다. osFoundry 에이전트끼리 단계 사이에 일을 넘기는 방식은 핸드오프 페이지 에 있다. 밑에 깔린 프로토콜은 MCP 용어 설명 을 보면 된다.

title: I Built an Interactive 3D Camera You Can Take Apart in Your Browser 📷
author: Jude
summary: I've been exploring Three.js and WebGL lately, experimenting with different ways to make websites more interactive. One thing I really enjoy about 3D on the web is that you're not limited to displaying objects. You can actually let people interact with them, explore them, and understand how things work. So I decided to build something around that idea. Meet Camera Lab — an interactive 3D experience where you can explore a DSLR camera, take it apart, and see what's happening inside. 📷 [Try the live demo here] What's interesting about it? Instead of simply displaying a 3D camera that rotates, I wanted people to be able to explore the engineering behind it. Here's what you can do: 🔄 Rotate and explore: View the camera from different angles, zoom in, and inspect the details. 🧩 Take it apart: Use the exploded-view slider to separate the camera's components and put everything back together. 🔍 Explore 25 components: Click individual parts to learn more about them, including the lens, shutter, mirror, sensor, and internal electronics. 👁️ X-ray mode: Look through the camera's exterior to see what's happening inside. 🎯 Guided exploration: Follow a step-by-step tour showing how light travels through a DSLR camera. 📸 Capture screenshots: Save a view of the 3D model directly from the experience. One of my favourite parts is the exploded view. Seeing the different components separate and come back together makes the whole experience much more interesting. 🛠️ What did I build it with? The main technologies behind the project are: Three.js / WebGL — 3D rendering and interactions React + TypeScript — Application structure and UI GSAP — Animations and transitions Tailwind CSS — Styling Vite — Development and build tooling Vercel — Deployment The camera model is generated using procedural 3D geometry rather than relying on a downloaded camera model. This made it possible to work with the components individually and create the interactive disassembly experience. 💡 Why I enjoyed building this What interests me most about Three.js is how it opens up a different approach to web development. A website doesn't always have to be a collection of pages, buttons, and forms. Sometimes it can be an experience. Projects like this make me want to keep exploring interactive product visualizations, 3D storytelling, and educational experiences on the web. title: How much data can a QR code actually hold?
author: Rahman
summary: Short answer: more than you'll ever need for a link, and less than you'd think once you care about scanning. Let's unpack it. It's a grid of modules A QR code is a square grid of little cells called modules. The spec defines 40 sizes, called versions: version 1 is 21x21 modules, version 40 is 177x177. The more data you encode, the higher the version the generator has to use, so the more modules get packed into the same printed square. The theoretical maximums At the largest version with the lightest error correction, a single QR code can hold roughly: 7,089 numeric digits 4,296 alphanumeric characters 2,953 bytes of raw binary Those are ceilings, not targets. Hitting them means a dense version-40 code that a phone struggles to read unless it's printed large and scanned up close. Error correction eats into the budget QR codes have four error-correction levels: L, M, Q, H, recovering roughly 7, 15, 25, and 30 percent of the code if it's damaged. Higher protection is great for stickers and logos, but it costs capacity: the recovery data lives in the same grid, so the more you reserve for resilience, the less room is left for your actual content. The practical takeaway You almost never want to approach these limits. A long URL or a full contact card bloats the version, shrinks every module at print size, and makes the code fragile. Keep the content short, or point the code at a short link that redirects. A low-version code has big, chunky modules that scan fast from across a room, and that's the whole game. I help build QRolling , so I'm not neutral, but this holds with any generator.

title: Orbura: a camera check-in that becomes a baseline — Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
author: Papa
summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge What I Built Orbura Companion — a consent-first camera check-in that turns the Presage SmartSpectra SDK into an about-a-minute wellness ritual, wired directly into Orbura , a longitudinal health platform that converts physiological signals into one safe action . The product architecture is split across two complimentary surfaces: Orbura Companion (Electron + @smartspectra/node-sdk at showcases/presage-smartspectra/ ) is the capture instrument . It owns the local camera stream, the explicit consent gate, the guided scan, and the live multi-channel physiological waveforms. Orbura Web Platform (Next.js at orbura.famile.xyz ) is the canonical record . Check-ins land securely as camera_vitals observations alongside wearable data, feeding autonomic recovery baselines, exception triage, and clinical continuity. The core thesis: A single reading is trivia — accumulation is health. Day 1 is a reading; Day 30 is a baseline. The Video Showcase Watch on YouTube (85-second film with full spatial cinematography, narration, and physiological research callouts) . The film demonstrates the complete loop from first principles: The Human Moment: Daily check-in at the kitchen table. On-Device Consent: Explicit privacy guarantee before camera hardware initializes. The Sensor Lock: Remote optical plethysmography (rPPG) locking onto micro-capillary vascular flushes across facial landmarks. Live Signal Extraction: Real-time extraction of autonomic Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia (RSA) into four live charts. The Payoff: 9 BR/min resolving into "Today's one action: Take ten slow breaths before your next meal." Longitudinal Record: 30 days of breathing waves tightening into an empirical personal recovery baseline. Scale of Opportunity: Over 3.8 billion existing cameras in pockets and laptops transformed into proactive health sensors. Visual Architecture & Live Product Flow 1. The On-Device Privacy Architecture Before a single video frame is captured, the user is presented with a clear privacy contract. Processing is performed in-memory on the user's Mac using the SmartSpectra SDK. Raw pixels, video, and facial landmarks are never stored or transmitted. The camera indicator remains visible, backed by a persistent "Live · Not recording" status. 2. Multi-Channel Signal Extraction (rPPG & RSA) Upon starting measurement, the SmartSpectra SDK initiates remote photoplethysmography. The interface visualizes four continuous physiological channels: Breathing Rate (BR/min) Raw Breathing Waveform (Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia) Pulse Rate (BPM) Arterial Pressure Trace Confidence and position metrics continuously guide the user through a dynamic SVG guide oval, turning vibrant green ( Ok — Hold still and record ) once optical lock is achieved. 3. The Payoff: One Manageable Action Most health dashboards dump endless charts on users, creating cognitive overload and anxiety. Orbura deliberately reduces the session to: Deterministic Vitals: Measured breathing rate and pulse. One Thing to Notice: An educational takeaway on vagal autonomic recovery. Today's One Action: A single, clinic-approved behavioral micro-step that fits into the user's day. 4. The Longitudinal Record (Day 1 → Day 30) When the user taps Save to Orbura , only numeric values and timestamps cross the boundary via an encrypted link token ( POST /api/vitals/check-in ). Over weeks, these check-ins establish an empirical baseline band. Deviations trigger proactive nudges or clinician review before minor stress compounds into chronic exhaustion. Code & Setup GitHub Repository: https://github.com/udirobert/orbura (Public) Companion App: showcases/presage-smartspectra/ — Electron + @smartspectra/node-sdk Web Platform & Bridge API: src/app/api/vitals/ (check-in, latest, link-token routes) and src/components/hrv/CameraVitalsPanel.tsx Demo Composition Code: showcases/presage-smartspectra/demo-video/ (Vite + WebCodecs composition engine) Running the Companion (Judges) git clone https://github.com/udirobert/orbura.git cd orbura/showcases/presage-smartspectra npm install # Add your Presage API key (or export SMARTSPECTRA_API_KEY) echo "YOUR_PRESAGE_API_KEY" > .smartspectra-key npm start Note: The companion runs standalone without an account (guests attribute to an ephemeral local device ID), so judges can test the full capture loop immediately without creating an account. Prize Categories Entering both hackathon categories: 1. Most Creative or Delightful Use Check-in as Ritual: We designed the interaction as a quiet, respectful morning ritual rather than clinical telemetry. Dynamic Feedback: From the breathing MiniOrb to the reactive guide oval and living baseline wave animations, motion design provides intuitive physiological feedback. Architectural Separation: Splitting the capture instrument (local Electron app) from the longitudinal record (web platform) creates an intuitive, modular product architecture. 2. Best Thoughtful Real-World Use GLP-1 Care Continuity: Designed to solve a massive real-world healthcare bottleneck: helping patients navigating chronic medication titration stay engaged without needing expensive, charged wearable hardware. Uncompromising Privacy: Real on-device processing. No raw images, no video recordings, and no facial landmark arrays ever touch a server or cloud bucket. Honest Feedback at Every Boundary: Thoughtful fallback states across camera permission denials, unlinked accounts, and variable lighting. Consent and Data Handling Disclosure Explicit Consent Gate: The camera stream is blocked until the user accepts the transparent privacy charter. On-Device rPPG: Photoplethysmography computation executes locally in-memory via the SmartSpectra SDK. Numbers-Only Sync: Only scalar metrics (breathing rate, pulse, HRV timestamp) leave the machine, and only upon explicit user tap on Save to Orbura . Wellness Scope: All outputs carry the SmartSpectra wellness disclaimer — intended strictly for wellness tracking, stress recovery, and habits, never clinical diagnosis or treatment. Built with Presage SmartSpectra SDK for the DEV Challenge. Code, setup guide, and documentation are open source on GitHub.

title: Runique 4.0: a typed admin, column-level permissions, and forms that write correctly
author: itsuki
summary: In June, I presented Runique 2.1 here, a Rust web framework inspired by Django, built on Axum, SeaORM, and Tera. Version 3.0 followed. Today, 4.0 is released, and this is the version where I didn't just add features: I reworked the three components everything else depends on: the admin, permissions, and forms. Here's what changes, and why. 1. The model remains the single source of truth This doesn't change; it's the starting point for everything: a model is declared once. use runique :: prelude :: * ; model! { Blog , table : "blog" , pk : id => Pk , enums : { BlogStatus : [ Draft = "Draft" , Published = "Published" , Archived = "Archived" ], }, { title : text [ required ], email : email [ required ], website : url [ nullable ], summary : textarea [ rows : 3 , required ], content : richtext [ rows : 15 , required ], status : choice [ enum ( BlogStatus ), default : "Draft" , required ], view_count : int [ nullable , default : 0 ], } } From this, the SeaORM entity, SQL migration, and a typed form are generated. Version 4.0 adds types ( audio , video ), and requires you to declare what was previously implicit: the precision of a decimal , the ON DELETE action of a foreign key. A decision that affects the data should not be made on your behalf. 2. An admin declared in Rust, checked by the compiler The old admin relied on a macro and generated code. It has been removed. The new one is a typed builder , ModelAdmin , where each column is named using the entity's Column enum: use runique :: prelude :: * ; fn blog () -> ModelAdmin < blog :: Entity > { use blog :: Column :: * ; ModelAdmin :: new () .list (| l | { l .display ([ Title , Email , Website , Status ]) .sortable ([ Title , Status ]) .search ([ Title , Summary ]) .filter ([ Status ]) .action ( Status , "Published" , "Publish" ) }) .form (| f | { f .fields ([ Title , Email , Website , Summary , Content , Status , ViewCount ]) .readonly ([ ViewCount ]) }) } A misspelled column, or one renamed in the model, will no longer compile. There are no longer any strings to keep synchronized with the schema, and no generation step: the admin is integrated into the application builder with .with_admin(admin::config) . What comes with it: multi-value filters, filter pagination, bulk actions, change history, and pages that can be overridden block by block, validated at startup (an unknown variable in an override is rejected before the first visitor arrives). 3. Permissions with a single entry point This is the core of 4.0. In an admin, the real question isn't "who can get in", but "who can read or modify which column of which table ". Runique 4.0 answers this with ranks and account-level permissions : Rank Role Superuser the developer, until delivery Director the day-to-day site administrator Admin a moderator: they only have what the director checks for them, table by table and column by column A rank can only be managed downwards, never on oneself, and is never a form field. The technical decision I'm most pleased with: all checks go through a single module , the gate ( auth::gate ). Every operation on protected data requires proof of the Authorized type, and only the gate knows how to create one: its constructor is not visible anywhere else. Writing without going through the gate does not compile. A missed permission check becomes a compilation error, not a vulnerability discovered in production. Permissions act directly on the SELECT itself: an unauthorized column is never read from the database, rather than simply being hidden from the display. 4. Forms that write correctly The form engine has been redesigned around one idea: what is validated is what gets written, in a single transaction . use runique :: prelude :: * ; pub async fn create_blog ( mut request : Request ) -> AppResult < Response > { let form : BlogForm = request .form ( "blog" ); let mut form = match ValidationForm :: try_form ( form , & request ) .await { Ok ( validated ) => validated .into_form (), Err ( form ) => { context_update! ( request => { "blog_form" => & form }); return request .render ( "blog/blog.html" ); } }; match form .save ( & request .engine.db ) .await { Ok ( _ ) => Ok ( Redirect :: to ( "/blog" ) .into_response ()), Err ( err ) => { // the database error is shown in the form, not as a 500 form .forms_mut () .database_error ( & err ); context_update! ( request => { "blog_form" => & form }); request .render ( "blog/blog.html" ) } } } Each form has a name ( request.form("blog") ). Two forms on the same page no longer get mixed up: only the one that was submitted is validated. save writes by itself, within a transaction. Uploaded files are moved between the database write and the commit: a rejected write leaves no orphaned files, and a file that cannot be moved rolls back the write. MediaField::image() , audio() , and video() check the file's content , not just its extension: a text file renamed to .mp4 is rejected. Upload limits are consistent from end to end: a field never accepts more than the server reads, and a request declared too large is rejected based on its headers, before a single byte is read. 5. Security, reviewed point by point Version 4.0 fixes issues found while auditing the framework, and I'd rather list them than keep quiet about them. A few examples: Session contents stored in the database are encrypted (XChaCha20-Poly1305, key derived from SECRET_KEY ); A form submitted from another site is rejected before reaching the handler ( Sec-Fetch-Site ), in addition to the CSRF token; "Forgot password" responds in the same amount of time regardless of whether an account exists; "Active" files ( .html , .svg , .js ...) are never accepted by a file field; An upload error message no longer reveals the server's directory structure. The complete list, with the severity of each issue, is available in SECURITY.md . 6. What this breaks A lot, honestly: this is a major release. The old admin is gone, the form API changes ( try_new becomes try_form , save replaces the before_save / after_save hooks), and the session table gains a column. Everything is detailed, step by step, in the 3.x → 4.0 migration guide . 7. What's next Version 4.1 will focus on makemigrations : generating all schema operations without a manual step (table deletions, actual ALTER operations when changing a type, relation tables, renames). The roadmap is public: ROADMAP.md . Try it [ dependencies ] runique = { version = "4.0" , features = [ "postgres" , "admin" ] } cargo install runique --features postgres runique new my_project Documentation (FR/EN): Documentation Source code: Github If you're coming from Django, I'd be curious to know what you're still missing. And if you're more into Rust, the Authorized proof system is something I'm particularly interested in hearing feedback about. All feedback is welcome.
